knownFor: A learned Alexandrian who led people out of a besieged quarter of Alexandria, became bishop of Laodicea in Syria, and wrote on how to fix the date of Easter.
shortDescription: Anatolius, a learned Christian of Alexandria, used a vote of the city council to get almost all the besieged out of the palace quarter of the city. He later became bishop of Laodicea in Syria and wrote a rule for finding the date of Easter, and centuries later both sides of a quarrel over Easter claimed him.
datesNote: No old source gives a year for his birth, for his becoming bishop or for his death, or ties a year to the siege he lived through. Eusebius says the synod held on the case of Paul of Samosata called him to Antioch, and that the believers at Laodicea kept him as their bishop as he passed through. Jerome says he flourished under the emperors Probus and Carus. The later 200s comes from the modern dating of those reigns.
placeNote: Alexandria, in Egypt, where he was born and lived through the siege of the palace quarter; Caesarea in Palestine, where he was made a second bishop; Laodicea in Syria, where he was bishop
role: Scholar of Alexandria, then bishop at Caesarea in Palestine and at Laodicea in Syria

keyWorks.title: Paschal Canons
keyWorks.about: his writings on finding Easter. Eusebius says that in his works he gave his views on the Passover in particular, and quotes a long extract. In it, the first month, whose fourteenth day is the Passover, must not be counted from a new moon before the spring equinox. The count runs on a cycle of nineteen years, and the rule, he says, was known to the Jews before Christ

keyWorks.title: Institutes of Arithmetic
keyWorks.about: ten books on arithmetic, which Eusebius and Jerome name. The Library does not hold them

keyWorks.title: The Paschal Canon, in Latin
keyWorks.about: a longer Latin book on Easter under his name, which allows the feast to be kept up to the moon's twentieth day. Columbanus, writing to Pope Gregory the Great, quoted words that stand in it as the words of Anatolius. Whether Anatolius wrote it is disputed

traces: Columbanus, an Irish abbot, wrote to Pope Gregory the Great against an Easter on the moon's 21st or 22nd day. He cited Anatolius, and quoted words from the Latin Easter book under his name. The words say that if the moon rises only at midnight, darkness rules over the light, and the feast of the Lord's resurrection is light.
To a synod of bishops in Gaul, Columbanus wrote that he trusted the tradition of his homeland, and Anatolius, over Victorius, who had written lately and in doubt.

Bede wrote that the northern Irish and the Picts kept Easter from the moon's fourteenth to its twentieth day, believing they followed the writings of Anatolius. Anyone skilled, he added, could very easily tell whether that was true.

At the synod at Whitby in 664, Colman, for the Irish side, said Anatolius had written that Easter was to be kept from the fourteenth to the twentieth. Wilfrid, for Rome's side, answered that Anatolius had set out a cycle of nineteen years, which the whole church of Christ kept.
Bede lists among his own works a letter on the leap year and the equinox, according to Anatolius.
Elias of Nisibis cites the words of Anatolius, bishop of Laodicea, to show that the spring equinox fell on the 22nd of Adar in his time. That was two days earlier, Elias says, than in Christ's time.
remembered: Eusebius says he "stood first among the ablest men of our time" in arithmetic, geometry, astronomy, logic and physics, and was at the head in rhetoric.
Jerome calls him a man of wonderful learning, and says the greatness of his genius can be seen from his book on the Passover and his ten books on arithmetic.
In a letter defending Christian writers' use of pagan learning, Jerome names Anatolius, chief priest of the church of Laodicea, among those whose books weave in the teachings of the philosophers.
Jerome's Chronicle, under the emperor Probus, says that Anatolius, bishop of Laodicea, learned in the teachings of the philosophers, was much spoken of. Bede's Greater Chronicle repeats it.
At Whitby, Colman called him "a holy man, and much commended in church history." Wilfrid called him "a most holy, learned, and commendable man", but said Colman's side did not keep his rules.
Barhadbeshabba lists Anatolius, bishop of Laodicea, among the teachers who lived in the land of the Romans. Michael the Syrian says he followed Eusebius at Laodicea and was famous.
Bar Hebraeus calls Eusebius, bishop of Laodicea, and Anatolius, both Alexandrians, true leaders in sacred and secular learning.

uncertain: The siege rests on report. Eusebius tells it as others told it to him ("They relate", "They say"), and gives no cause for the siege and no year.

The cause of the war. Eusebius says only that the rest of the city was allied with the Roman army. Rufinus calls it a war that broke out among the citizens of Alexandria. Jerome's Chronicle, under the first year of the emperor Claudius, says the palace quarter, besieged for many years, was at last destroyed. No old source says this is the siege Eusebius tells.

Rufinus, in his Latin version of Eusebius a century later, tells the siege in other terms. He has Anatolius in the part of the city loyal to Rome, going to the Roman commander himself and receiving the refugees with a parent's and a doctor's care. His speech asks only that all unfit for war be let out of the gates, and Rufinus adds that he freed the city from famine and war alike. Eusebius gives the message and the welcome to the deacon outside the lines.

The school. Eusebius gives only the report that the citizens asked him to found a school of Aristotle's philosophy. Rufinus says that he was trained from boyhood, so that all the learned men and philosophers of Alexandria made him teach logic. Neither says he held a church office there.
His subjects. Eusebius lists arithmetic, geometry, astronomy, logic, physics and rhetoric. Jerome has grammar in place of physics.

The years. No held old source gives a year for his birth, his becoming bishop or his death, or ties a year to the siege he lived through. Jerome says he flourished under Probus and Carus, and his Chronicle names him under Probus. Elias of Nisibis says he lived in the time of the emperor Gallus. Modern editors give years of their own reckoning, which differ.

The synod. Eusebius says only that the synod on Paul's case called him to Antioch and that the believers at Laodicea kept him as he passed through. No old source says whether he ever reached the synod. That Paul taught that Christ was by nature an ordinary man is the charge Eusebius gives.
His death. No held old source tells how, where or when he died. Eusebius says only that after him Stephen was the last bishop of Laodicea before the persecution.
The Easter book. No old source says where or when he wrote it. Eusebius quotes only part of it.

The nineteen years. Wilfrid credits Anatolius with setting out a cycle of nineteen years. Abbot Ceolfrid's letter, which Bede copies, says the nineteen-year cycle began in the time of the apostles, at Rome and in Egypt, and does not name him.

The Latin book. A longer Latin book on Easter carries his name. It was first printed in 1634. Whether he wrote it, no old source says, and modern scholars disagree: some take it for an early translation of his own work, others for a later forgery.

What his days of the moon meant. Colman says Anatolius wrote that Easter was to be kept from the fourteenth to the twentieth. The Latin book under his name allows the celebration to be extended to the moon's twentieth. Wilfrid says Anatolius counted in the Egyptian way, so that his fourteenth was the fifteenth by evening and his twentieth the twenty-first. He adds that Colman's side sometimes kept Easter before the full moon. Bede says a skilled reader can tell whether the Irish truly followed him. No old source says which text either man drew on.

A Syriac chronicle, in its Latin version, calls him a teacher at Laodicea after Eusebius, an Alexandrian by birth. It says he taught that the months begin on the eighteenth of Adar, and that the count comes round again after nineteen years. The extract Eusebius quotes puts the new moon at the head of the cycle on the 26th of the Egyptian month Phamenoth, the 22nd of the Macedonian month Dystrus.

Socrates, writing against the Easter of Sabbatius, gives the rule that the ancient Hebrews sacrificed after the spring equinox. He cites Eusebius, and Philo, Josephus and Aristobulus, writers the extract from Anatolius names, but does not name Anatolius.
The books on arithmetic. The Ante-Nicene Fathers prints fragments of books on arithmetic under his name, taken from a modern collection. That they are his rests on modern editors.

briefReferences: Eusebius, Church History VII.32.8 to 9, tr. Arthur McGiffert, with the Greek ed. Eduard Schwartz: the bread run out, hunger harder to bear than the enemy outside, and the speech to the city council, rendered from the Greek.

Church History VII.32.6: born in Alexandria; first among the men of his time in arithmetic, geometry, astronomy, logic, physics and rhetoric; the report that the citizens asked him to found a school of Aristotle's philosophy. Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 73: he flourished under Probus and Carus.
Church History VII.32.7: the siege, one of his many deeds, told as others told it.
Church History VII.32.8 to 9: the rest of the city allied with the Roman army; the deacon outside the lines, known to the Roman general, winning safety for deserters.
Church History VII.32.9 to 10: the council, his call for peace with Rome and its anger, the argument to feed only men and youths, his vote, and the council's agreement.

Church History VII.32.11: almost all the besieged saved, the church's people first, many more beyond the decree in women's clothes, by night to the Roman camp, where the deacon took them in like a father and a doctor.

Church History VII.32.21, with VII.32.5 to 6 and VII.27.2: the bishop of Caesarea in Palestine making him a second bishop to succeed him; the bishops at Antioch calling him, and Paul's teaching as Eusebius gives it; the believers at Laodicea, whose bishop, the same deacon, had died, keeping him.

Church History VII.32.13 to 16, the extract from his Paschal Canons: the first month not counted from a new moon before the spring equinox, the mistake of those who do, the nineteen-year cycle, and the rule known to the Jews before Christ.

Columbanus, letter to Pope Gregory the Great, tr. James Barmby: the Irish Easter defended against an Easter past the moon's twentieth day, and the darkness argument from the Latin Easter book under Anatolius's name, whose words stand in the Paschal Canon (Latin version) in the Ante-Nicene Fathers.

Bede, Ecclesiastical History III.25, tr. Giles, with the Latin ed. Plummer: the meeting at Whitby in 664, in Abbess Hild's monastery; Colman's claim for the fourteenth to the twentieth; Wilfrid's answer, rendered from the Latin, and the cycle of nineteen years. Bede V.23: the year 731.

Bede, Ecclesiastical History III.3, tr. Giles, with the Latin ed. Plummer: the northern Irish and Picts believing they followed the writings of Anatolius, and anyone skilled able to tell very easily whether that was true.

timeline.headline: A learned man of Alexandria
timeline.witness: Eusebius of Caesarea, a younger man of the same time

lines.text: Born in Alexandria.
Ranked first among the ablest men of his time in arithmetic, geometry, astronomy, logic and physics, and at the head in rhetoric.
lines.note: Jerome has grammar in place of physics.

lines.text: The citizens of Alexandria are reported to have asked him to found a school of Aristotle's philosophy.
lines.note: A report only. Rufinus, a century later, says all the learned men and philosophers of Alexandria made him teach logic.

timeline.headline: He gets the besieged out of the palace quarter
timeline.witness: Eusebius of Caesarea, from what others told him

lines.text: During the siege of the palace quarter of Alexandria he does many deeds, for which all those in high office honor him. Eusebius tells one.
lines.note: Eusebius's word for the quarter is Pyrucheium; his translator's note explains it as the quarter that held the royal palaces and the citadel.

lines.text: The bread runs out, and the famine is harder to bear than the enemy outside.
The rest of the city is allied with the Roman army. Anatolius sends word of the starving to Eusebius, a deacon of the church in the free part, whose name has reached the Roman general.
lines.note: Rufinus puts Anatolius himself in the part loyal to Rome and has him go to the Roman commander.

lines.text: The deacon asks the Roman commander, as the greatest favor, to grant safety to deserters, and wins it.
Anatolius calls the city council and first urges all to make peace with Rome. They grow angry.
He argues that the old women, children and old men, the crippled and the maimed, should be sent out of the gates. The city should feed only men and youths.
Rising first, he votes that all not needed for the army, men or women, should leave, since if they stay they will starve. The council agrees.
lines.reference: Eusebius, Church History VII.32.10 to 11, cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 42745-42753

lines.text: Under cover of the decree he saves almost all the besieged, the church's people first, then others of every age. Many more beyond the decree go too, secretly dressed in women's clothes. They go out of the gates to the Roman camp.
At the camp the deacon takes them all in, like a father and a doctor, and nurses them back to health.
lines.note: Rufinus gives this welcome to Anatolius, and adds that he freed the city from famine and war alike.

timeline.headline: Bishop at Caesarea, then at Laodicea

lines.text: Eusebius says the church of Laodicea had two such pastors in turn, the deacon Eusebius and Anatolius, who came there from Alexandria after the war.
The deacon goes to Syria over the affair of Paul of Samosata, and is kept there as bishop of Laodicea.
Theotecnus, bishop of Caesarea in Palestine, makes Anatolius a bishop, meaning him to succeed him at his death. For a short time the two lead that church together.
The synod held on the case of Paul of Samosata, bishop of Antioch, calls Anatolius to Antioch. Eusebius says Paul taught that Christ was by nature an ordinary man.
lines.reference: Eusebius, Church History VII.32.21 and VII.27.2, cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 42928-42938; 41838-41840
lines.note: No old source says whether Anatolius reached the synod.

lines.text: Passing through Laodicea, whose bishop, the deacon Eusebius, has died, he is kept there by the believers as their bishop: one good man, Eusebius says, following another.
lines.reference: Eusebius, Church History VII.32.21 and VII.32.6, cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 42938-42940; 42683-42684

lines.when: Under the emperors Probus and Carus
lines.text: Jerome says that Anatolius of Alexandria, bishop of Laodicea in Syria, flourished then.
lines.reference: Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 73, cic/texts/npnf203_theodoret-jerome-gennadius-rufinus.xml lines 40932-40934
lines.note: Elias of Nisibis, much later, says he lived in the time of the emperor Gallus.

lines.text: After Anatolius dies, Stephen is the last bishop of Laodicea before the persecution.
lines.note: No held old source tells how, where or when he died.

timeline.headline: His writings on Easter and on arithmetic
timeline.witness: Anatolius's own words, as Eusebius quotes them

lines.text: He writes few works, Eusebius says, and in them gives his views on the Passover above all.
lines.note: No old source says where or when he wrote.

lines.text: In the first year of his cycle, he sets the new moon of the first month on the 26th of the Egyptian month Phamenoth. That new moon is the beginning of every cycle of nineteen years.
lines.reference: Anatolius, Paschal Canons, in Eusebius, Church History VII.32.14, cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 42788-42803

lines.text: The first segment of the sun's yearly path begins at the spring equinox. He writes that those who put the first month, and the Passover's fourteenth day, in the segment before it make no small mistake.
lines.reference: Anatolius, Paschal Canons, in Eusebius, Church History VII.32.15, cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 42805-42817

lines.text: He says the rule is not his own, since the Jews knew it before Christ. Philo, Josephus, Musaeus, the two Agathobuli and Aristobulus, he writes, say the Passover is sacrificed after the spring equinox.
lines.reference: Anatolius, Paschal Canons, in Eusebius, Church History VII.32.16 to 17, cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 42819-42868

lines.text: He writes the Institutes of Arithmetic, in ten books.
lines.reference: Eusebius, Church History VII.32.20, cic/texts/npnf201_eusebius-church-history-life-of-constantine.xml lines 42917-42918; Jerome, Lives of Illustrious Men 73, cic/texts/npnf203_theodoret-jerome-gennadius-rufinus.xml lines 40936-40938

timeline.headline: Claimed in the Easter quarrel of the Irish and Rome

lines.when: While Gregory the Great was pope
lines.text: Columbanus, an Irish abbot, writes to Gregory against an Easter on the moon's 21st or 22nd day. He cites Anatolius, a man of wonderful learning, as Jerome says, whose writings Eusebius set into his Church History. He quotes words from the Latin Easter book under his name: when the moon rises only at midnight, darkness rules over the light.
lines.reference: Columbanus, letter to Gregory the Great, cic/texts/npnf213_gregory-great-ephraim-syrus-aphrahat.xml lines 4320-4355
lines.note: The words Columbanus quotes stand in the Latin Paschal Canon under Anatolius's name, not in the Greek extract Eusebius keeps.

lines.text: Columbanus writes to a synod of bishops in Gaul that he trusts his homeland's tradition, and Anatolius, over Victorius.
lines.reference: Columbanus, letter to a synod of Gaul, cic/texts/paulus-emeritanus-braulio-sisebut-pl80-lat_migne1863.txt lines 20791-20797

lines.text: A synod meets in the monastery at Whitby, where Abbess Hild presides. Bishop Colman, who leads the Irish side, asks whether Anatolius, a holy man much commended in church history, went against the law and the Gospel when he wrote that Easter was to be kept from the fourteenth to the twentieth.
lines.reference: Bede, Ecclesiastical History III.25 to 26, cic/texts/bede_ecclesiastical-history-english-people_giles1903.txt lines 7956-7967; 8117-8121; 8236-8237

lines.text: Wilfrid, for Rome's side, answers that Anatolius set out a cycle of nineteen years, which the whole church of Christ keeps. He adds that Anatolius counted his days in the Egyptian way, from evening.
lines.reference: Bede, Ecclesiastical History III.25 to 26, cic/texts/bede_ecclesiastical-history-english-people_giles1903.txt lines 8134-8150; 8236-8237

lines.text: The king rules for Peter, who holds the keys of heaven, and all present agree. Colman leaves, taking with him those who will not accept the Easter agreed there.
lines.reference: Bede, Ecclesiastical History III.25 to 26, cic/texts/bede_ecclesiastical-history-english-people_giles1903.txt lines 8195-8237

lines.text: Bede writes that the northern Irish and the Picts believed they followed the writings of Anatolius, and that anyone skilled could very easily tell whether that was true.

timeline.headline: His name kept in chronicles and reckonings

lines.text: Jerome names him in a letter among Christian writers whose books weave in the teachings of the philosophers, and his Chronicle praises him under Probus.

lines.text: Bede's Greater Chronicle repeats Jerome's praise of him.
Bede lists among his own works a letter on the leap year and the equinox, according to Anatolius.
Barhadbeshabba lists him among the teachers in the land of the Romans; a Syriac chronicle calls him a teacher at Laodicea after Eusebius.

Michael the Syrian calls him famous, and Bar Hebraeus calls him and Eusebius true leaders in sacred and secular learning.
